title: What is a Computer?
explanation: A computer is a machine that follows instructions. It takes information in, processes it, and gives information out. Your phone, laptop, and even a calculator are all computers.
analogy: A computer is like a very fast, very obedient assistant who can only follow exact instructions.
example: You type a message (input), the computer sends it (process), your friend sees it (output).
why_it_matters: Everything digital runs on computers. Understanding them helps you understand the modern world.
checkpoint_question: What are the three things a computer does with information?
expected_answer: A computer takes information in (input), processes it, and gives information out (output).
common_mistake: Thinking computers are 'smart'. They only do exactly what they're told - nothing more.
key_insight: Computers are incredibly fast but incredibly literal. They do exactly what you say, not what you mean.

title: Hardware vs Software
explanation: Hardware is the physical stuff you can touch - the screen, keyboard, chips inside. Software is the instructions that tell hardware what to do. You can't touch software.
analogy: Hardware is like your body. Software is like your thoughts and decisions that control what your body does.
example: Your phone (hardware) runs Instagram (software). Same phone can run different apps.
why_it_matters: Knowing this difference helps you understand what can be changed with an update vs what needs new equipment.
checkpoint_question: Can you change software without buying new hardware?
expected_answer: Yes! Software can be updated, installed, or removed on the same hardware. That's why your phone gets new features through updates.
common_mistake: Thinking you need a new computer when software is slow. Often, the software just needs fixing.
key_insight: Software is what makes hardware useful. A phone without apps is just an expensive paperweight.

title: The Language of Computers: Binary
explanation: Computers only understand two things: on and off. We write this as 1 (on) and 0 (off). This is called binary. Everything - photos, music, apps - is stored as patterns of 1s and 0s.
analogy: Binary is like a light switch. You can only flip it on or off. But with millions of switches, you can create complex patterns.
example: The letter 'A' is stored as 01000001. The number 5 is stored as 00000101.
why_it_matters: Understanding binary helps you see how computers turn simple on/off signals into everything digital.
checkpoint_question: Why do computers use only 1s and 0s?
expected_answer: Because electronic circuits can only be on or off. It's the simplest, most reliable way for machines to store and process information.
common_mistake: Thinking binary is complicated. It's actually the simplest possible system - just on and off!
key_insight: A single 1 or 0 is called a 'bit'. 8 bits make a 'byte'. Your phone might have 128 billion bytes (gigabytes) of storage.

title: Counting in Binary
explanation: In binary, you only have two digits (0 and 1) instead of ten (0-9). So you run out of digits faster and need to add a new place. 0, 1, then 10 (which means 2), 11 (means 3), 100 (means 4).
analogy: It's like counting on your fingers if you only had 2 fingers. You'd run out fast and need a new way to track bigger numbers.
example: Binary 10 = 2 in normal numbers. Binary 100 = 4. Binary 1000 = 8. Each new place doubles the value.
why_it_matters: This explains why computer storage comes in sizes like 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 - they're all powers of 2.
checkpoint_question: What does binary 11 equal in regular numbers?
expected_answer: 3. The right digit means 1, the left digit means 2. So 1 + 2 = 3.
common_mistake: Reading binary '10' as ten. In binary, 10 means two!
key_insight: Each position in binary is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128...

title: What is Programming?
explanation: Programming is writing instructions that a computer can follow. These instructions are written in special languages that both humans and computers can understand.
analogy: Programming is like writing a very detailed recipe. Every step must be exact, or the dish won't turn out right.
example: To make a computer say 'Hello', you write: print('Hello'). The computer reads this and displays 'Hello' on screen.
why_it_matters: Programming is how we tell computers what to do. Every app, website, and game was created by programming.
checkpoint_question: Why do programmers need to be very precise?
expected_answer: Computers follow instructions exactly as written. A small mistake (like a typo) can cause the whole program to fail or do the wrong thing.
common_mistake: Thinking you need to be a math genius to program. Most programming is about logic and clear thinking.
key_insight: The first program most people write just displays 'Hello, World!' It's a tradition since 1978!

title: Programming Languages
explanation: Just like humans speak different languages, there are many programming languages. Python is easy to read. JavaScript runs websites. Swift builds iPhone apps. They all do the same thing - give instructions to computers.
analogy: Programming languages are like human languages. French and English say the same ideas differently. Python and JavaScript tell computers the same things differently.
example: Saying 'Hello' in Python: print('Hello'). In JavaScript: console.log('Hello'). Different words, same result.
why_it_matters: Different languages are better for different jobs. Knowing this helps you pick the right tool.
checkpoint_question: Do all programming languages do the same basic thing?
expected_answer: Yes! All programming languages give instructions to computers. They just have different styles and strengths for different tasks.
common_mistake: Thinking one language is 'best'. Each has strengths. Python is great for beginners, JavaScript for websites, Swift for iPhones.
key_insight: Learning one language makes learning others easier. The core ideas are the same - only the syntax (spelling) changes.

title: What is an Algorithm?
explanation: An algorithm is a set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem or complete a task. It's like a recipe - follow the steps in order and you get the result.
analogy: A recipe for making a sandwich is an algorithm. Step 1: Get bread. Step 2: Add filling. Step 3: Close the sandwich.
example: Algorithm to find a word in a dictionary: 1) Open to middle. 2) Is your word before or after? 3) Go to that half. 4) Repeat until found.
why_it_matters: Every program is built from algorithms. Learning to think in steps is the core skill of computer science.
checkpoint_question: Write an algorithm for brushing your teeth.
expected_answer: 1) Pick up toothbrush. 2) Put toothpaste on brush. 3) Brush each section of teeth. 4) Rinse mouth. 5) Rinse brush. Any clear step-by-step answer works!
common_mistake: Skipping steps that seem 'obvious'. Computers need EVERY step - they won't assume anything.
key_insight: The best algorithms are simple, clear, and work every time - no matter what input they receive.

title: Good vs Bad Algorithms
explanation: Some algorithms are faster than others. Finding a name in a phone book by checking every page is slow. Opening to the middle and narrowing down is fast. Both work, but one is much better.
analogy: Finding a book in a library: you could check every shelf (slow), or use the catalog system (fast). Same result, very different effort.
example: Finding 'Smith' in 1000 names: Checking one by one might take 1000 looks. The halving method takes about 10 looks.
why_it_matters: When computers handle millions of items, good algorithms save hours or days of time.
checkpoint_question: Why does the 'halving' method work so much faster?
expected_answer: Each step eliminates half the remaining options. After 10 halvings, you've narrowed 1000 items down to 1. Checking one-by-one might need all 1000 checks.
common_mistake: Assuming the first working solution is good enough. Often a better algorithm exists.
key_insight: This 'halving' approach is called Binary Search. It's one of the most important algorithms in computer science.

title: True and False
explanation: Computers make decisions based on true or false questions. Is 5 greater than 3? True. Is 2 equal to 7? False. Programs use these yes/no answers to decide what to do next.
analogy: It's like playing 20 Questions. Each question has a yes or no answer, and the answers guide what happens next.
example: Is the user logged in? If TRUE, show their profile. If FALSE, show the login page.
why_it_matters: All computer decisions come down to true/false questions. Understanding this helps you think like a programmer.
checkpoint_question: What would a computer answer to: Is 10 equal to 10?
expected_answer: True. 10 is equal to 10, so the answer is true.
common_mistake: Confusing 'equals' (==) with 'assign' (=). Checking if things match vs setting a value are different.
code:
# True or False?
5 > 3    # True
2 == 7   # False
10 <= 10 # True
key_insight: In programming, true/false values are called 'booleans', named after mathematician George Boole.

title: AND, OR, NOT
explanation: You can combine true/false questions. AND means both must be true. OR means at least one must be true. NOT flips true to false (or false to true).
analogy: AND: You need a ticket AND an ID to enter. OR: You can pay with cash OR card. NOT: If the door is NOT locked, you can open it.
example: Is it sunny AND warm? Both must be true. Is it sunny OR warm? Just one needs to be true.
why_it_matters: Programs use AND, OR, NOT constantly to make complex decisions from simple yes/no questions.
checkpoint_question: If it's raining (true) AND cold (true), what's the result?
expected_answer: True. With AND, both conditions must be true. Since both 'raining' and 'cold' are true, the whole thing is true.
common_mistake: Mixing up AND and OR. AND is stricter (both needed). OR is looser (just one needed).
code:
# AND - both must be true
True and True   # True
True and False  # False

# OR - at least one true
True or False   # True
False or False  # False

# NOT - flips the value
not True   # False
not False  # True
key_insight: These simple operations (AND, OR, NOT) are the building blocks of all computer logic, from games to AI.

title: What is Data?
explanation: Data is information stored in a computer. It can be numbers (42), text ('Hello'), images, sounds, or anything else. Computers store, organize, and process data.
analogy: Data is like ingredients in a kitchen. You can store them, organize them, and combine them to create something useful.
example: Your contacts app stores data: names, phone numbers, emails. A photo app stores image data. A music app stores audio data.
why_it_matters: Everything computers do involves data. Understanding data is understanding what computers work with.
checkpoint_question: Give three examples of data you create every day.
expected_answer: Examples: text messages, photos, search queries, likes on posts, location data, purchase history - any information you generate or input.
common_mistake: Thinking data is only numbers. Text, images, videos, and sounds are all data too.
key_insight: Big companies are valuable partly because of all the data they've collected. Data is often called 'the new oil'.

title: Types of Data
explanation: Data comes in different types. Numbers (1, 2, 3.14) for math. Text ('Hello') for words. Booleans (true/false) for yes/no. Each type has different uses.
analogy: Like different containers for different things: jars for liquids, boxes for solids. You use the right type for the right data.
example: Age is a number: 25. Name is text: 'Alice'. Is member? is boolean: true. Price is a number: 9.99.
why_it_matters: Using the right data type prevents errors. You can't do math on text or spell words with numbers.
checkpoint_question: What type would you use for someone's email address?
expected_answer: Text (also called a 'string'). Email addresses contain letters, numbers, and symbols like @ and . which are stored as text.
common_mistake: Storing phone numbers as actual numbers. They should be text - you'll never do math on them, and leading zeros matter.
code:
# Different data types
age = 25           # Number (integer)
price = 19.99      # Number (decimal)
name = 'Alice'     # Text (string)
is_member = True   # Boolean
key_insight: Programming languages are strict about types. Adding a number to text causes an error - you must convert first.

title: How Computers Store Text
explanation: Every letter, number, and symbol has a code number. 'A' is 65, 'B' is 66, 'a' is 97. This system is called ASCII. Modern computers use Unicode, which has codes for every character in every language, plus emojis!
analogy: Like Morse code: each letter has a pattern. Computers just use numbers instead of dots and dashes.
example: 'Hi' is stored as: 72 (H), 105 (i). The computer sees numbers, but displays letters based on those codes.
why_it_matters: This explains why text files are small (just numbers), and why sometimes you see weird characters when codes get confused.
checkpoint_question: Why do we need special codes like Unicode?
expected_answer: ASCII only has 128 codes - not enough for all world languages. Unicode has over 140,000 characters: Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, emojis, and more. It makes global communication possible.
common_mistake: Thinking emojis are images. They're actually text characters with code numbers, like letters!
code:
# Character codes
print(ord('A'))  # 65
print(ord('a'))  # 97
print(chr(65))   # 'A'
print(ord('😀')) # 128512 (Unicode)
key_insight: UTF-8 is the most common encoding. It uses 1 byte for English letters, more bytes for other characters. Efficient and universal.

title: The CPU: The Brain
explanation: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the brain of the computer. It executes instructions - billions per second. It reads an instruction, performs it, reads the next, repeats. Everything your computer does flows through the CPU.
analogy: The CPU is like a chef following recipes incredibly fast - reading one step, doing it, reading the next, over and over billions of times per second.
example: You click a button. The CPU runs millions of instructions: check mouse position, is it over button? yes, run button's code, update screen...
why_it_matters: CPU speed affects how fast your computer runs. Understanding this helps you understand performance.
checkpoint_question: Why are modern CPUs measured in GHz (gigahertz)?
expected_answer: GHz measures billions of cycles per second. A 3 GHz CPU can do about 3 billion tiny operations per second. Higher GHz generally means faster processing.
common_mistake: Thinking higher GHz always means faster. Modern CPUs do more work per cycle, so a 3 GHz new CPU beats a 4 GHz old one.
key_insight: Modern CPUs have multiple 'cores' - like multiple brains. A 4-core CPU can do 4 things truly simultaneously.

title: Memory: RAM vs Storage
explanation: RAM is fast but temporary - it's cleared when power is off. Storage (SSD/hard drive) is permanent but slower. Programs load from storage into RAM to run fast, then save back to storage to keep data.
analogy: RAM is your desk - what you're actively working on. Storage is your filing cabinet - where you keep things long-term but must retrieve them to use.
example: Open a document: copied from storage to RAM. Edit it: changes in RAM. Save: copies back to storage. Close without saving: RAM version lost.
why_it_matters: More RAM means more programs running smoothly. Understanding this helps you choose computers and troubleshoot slowness.
checkpoint_question: Why does your computer slow down when you open too many programs?
expected_answer: Each program uses RAM. When RAM fills up, the computer uses slower storage as overflow (called 'swapping'). This makes everything slow because storage is much slower than RAM.
common_mistake: Confusing RAM with storage. '8GB RAM' and '256GB storage' are different. RAM is for active work, storage is for keeping files.
key_insight: SSDs are much faster than old hard drives. That's why modern computers feel snappier - storage is less of a bottleneck.

title: How the Internet Works
explanation: The internet is a network of connected computers worldwide. Data travels in small pieces called packets, hopping between computers until reaching the destination. It's designed to find paths around failures.
analogy: The internet is like a postal system. Letters (packets) travel between post offices (routers), getting passed along until they reach the destination.
example: You load a webpage: browser sends request across many networks to the server. Server sends page back in pieces. Browser assembles and displays it.
why_it_matters: Everything online depends on this. Understanding it helps you understand why some things are fast/slow and how data travels.
checkpoint_question: Why is data sent in small packets instead of one big piece?
expected_answer: If one big transmission fails, you restart everything. With packets, only failed packets resend. Plus, packets can take different routes and arrive in any order - more reliable and efficient.
common_mistake: Thinking the internet is one company or system. It's thousands of networks agreeing to connect and pass traffic to each other.
key_insight: The internet was designed by the military to survive attacks. If one path is destroyed, data routes around the damage.

title: Computational Thinking
explanation: Computational thinking is approaching problems like a computer scientist. Break big problems into smaller pieces (decomposition). Find patterns. Focus on important details, ignore the rest (abstraction). Design step-by-step solutions (algorithms).
analogy: It's like being a detective: break the case into clues (decomposition), notice patterns, focus on what matters, build a theory step by step.
example: Planning a party: decompose (food, invites, music), find patterns (what worked before), abstract (focus on key tasks), create plan (step-by-step to-do list).
why_it_matters: These skills apply beyond programming. They help you solve complex problems in any field.
checkpoint_question: How would you decompose 'building a website'?
expected_answer: Break into: design layout, write content, choose colors/fonts, build each page, add navigation, test on different devices, deploy online. Each piece is more manageable than the whole.
common_mistake: Trying to solve big problems all at once. Break them down first - always.
key_insight: Computational thinking isn't about computers - it's a problem-solving approach that predates and goes beyond technology.

title: Abstraction: Hiding Complexity
explanation: Abstraction means hiding complicated details behind a simple interface. You use a car without knowing how the engine works. You use apps without knowing the code. Each layer hides the complexity below it.
analogy: A TV remote abstracts the TV. You press 'volume up' without knowing the circuits inside. The button is simple; the electronics are complex and hidden.
example: Sending a text: you type and tap send (simple). Behind that: encryption, network protocols, cell towers, routing, decryption (complex). Abstraction hides all that.
why_it_matters: Abstraction is how we manage complexity. Without it, we couldn't build or use modern technology.
checkpoint_question: Why is abstraction essential for building software?
expected_answer: Without abstraction, every programmer would need to understand every detail - hardware, networking, graphics, everything. Abstraction lets people focus on their layer while trusting layers below work correctly.
common_mistake: Thinking abstractions are 'cheating'. They're essential. Even the best programmers rely on abstractions built by others.
code:
# Abstraction example
# Low level: write bytes to network socket
# Higher level: http library handles details
# Highest level: just call
response = requests.get('https://example.com')
# All the complexity is hidden!
key_insight: Leaky abstractions: sometimes the hidden complexity leaks through, causing unexpected behavior. Good abstractions minimize this.

title: How We Got Here: Computing History
explanation: Early computers filled rooms and had less power than your watch. The transistor (1947) made them smaller. Integrated circuits (1958) put thousands of transistors on a chip. Moore's Law: computing power doubles roughly every two years.
analogy: Imagine if cars improved like computers: a car from 1970 would now go millions of miles per hour and cost pennies. That's how dramatic computer improvement has been.
example: ENIAC (1945): 30 tons, 18,000 vacuum tubes. Your phone: 6 ounces, billions of transistors. More power in your pocket than NASA had for the moon landing.
why_it_matters: Understanding history shows why computing changed everything and suggests how it might continue evolving.
checkpoint_question: What is Moore's Law?
expected_answer: The observation that the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every two years, making computers increasingly powerful and cheap. It's held true for decades.
common_mistake: Thinking Moore's Law is a physical law. It's an observation that's held remarkably well but may slow down as we hit physics limits.
key_insight: We may be hitting physical limits - transistors are approaching atomic scale. Quantum computing and other technologies may be the next leap.

title: What Computers Cannot Do
explanation: Some problems are mathematically impossible for any computer to solve. The 'halting problem' proves no program can determine if any other program will finish or run forever. These limits are fundamental, not just current technology.
analogy: Like trying to create a sentence that's true about itself being false. Some things are logically impossible, not just hard.
example: You can't build an antivirus that perfectly detects all malware - that would require solving the halting problem, which is proven impossible.
why_it_matters: Understanding limits prevents chasing impossible goals. It also shows computer science is about fundamental truths, not just technology.
checkpoint_question: Why can't we build a perfect program-checker that detects all bugs?
expected_answer: Due to the halting problem. To check if any program is bug-free, you'd need to determine if it ever misbehaves - including whether it runs forever. This is mathematically proven impossible.
common_mistake: Thinking enough computing power can solve anything. Some problems have logical limits, not just practical ones.
key_insight: Alan Turing proved the halting problem is unsolvable in 1936 - before electronic computers existed! Pure mathematical reasoning.

title: Boolean Logic: True or False
explanation: Computers make decisions using boolean logic - statements that are either TRUE or FALSE. AND means both must be true. OR means at least one must be true. NOT flips true to false.
analogy: Like answering yes/no questions. 'Is it raining AND cold?' requires both. 'Is it raining OR snowing?' needs just one.
example: Login check: (username correct) AND (password correct) must BOTH be true. If either is false, login fails.
why_it_matters: Every if-statement, every search filter, every decision a computer makes uses boolean logic. It's the foundation of all computing decisions.
checkpoint_question: If A is TRUE and B is FALSE, what is A AND B? What is A OR B?
expected_answer: A AND B is FALSE (both must be true). A OR B is TRUE (at least one is true).
common_mistake: Confusing AND with OR. AND is stricter - everything must be true. OR is lenient - anything can be true.
key_insight: All computer circuits are built from AND, OR, and NOT gates. Complex processors are just billions of these simple logic operations.

title: Files: Containers for Data
explanation: A file is a named collection of data stored on disk. The file extension (.jpg, .mp3, .pdf) hints at what's inside and how to read it. Files are organized in folders (directories) in a tree structure.
analogy: Files are like labeled boxes. The label tells you what's inside (photo, document, song). Folders are like shelves organizing the boxes.
example: photo.jpg is an image file. report.pdf is a document. song.mp3 is audio. The extension tells apps how to interpret the 1s and 0s inside.
why_it_matters: Every piece of data you use - documents, photos, apps - is stored in files. Understanding files helps you organize and manage your digital life.
checkpoint_question: What happens if you rename photo.jpg to photo.txt?
expected_answer: The data inside doesn't change - it's still an image. But programs might get confused because .txt suggests text. You'd see garbled characters instead of the image.
common_mistake: Thinking file extensions change the content. They're just hints for programs - the actual data stays the same.
key_insight: File formats are agreements on how to structure data. A .png and .jpg both store images, but organize the bytes differently.

title: Compression: Making Files Smaller
explanation: Compression shrinks files by finding patterns and representing them more efficiently. Lossless keeps everything perfect (ZIP). Lossy throws away data you won't notice (JPEG, MP3) for much smaller files.
analogy: Like abbreviations. 'BTW' is shorter than 'by the way' but means the same (lossless). A summary loses details but captures the main idea (lossy).
example: A photo: RAW is huge but perfect. JPEG is much smaller but loses tiny details you can't see. For sharing online, JPEG is usually fine.
why_it_matters: Compression makes streaming, downloads, and storage practical. Without it, a single movie would be hundreds of gigabytes.
checkpoint_question: Why would you use lossless compression for a document but lossy for a photo?
expected_answer: Documents need every character exact - losing a digit changes meaning. Photos can lose tiny details humans can't perceive, making much smaller files without visible quality loss.
common_mistake: Re-compressing lossy files. Each JPEG save loses more quality. Keep originals and only compress once for sharing.
key_insight: Video streaming works because of compression. Netflix uses about 3GB per hour in HD - uncompressed would be over 100GB.

title: How Screens Display Images
explanation: Screens are grids of tiny dots called pixels. Each pixel has red, green, and blue lights that mix to create any color. Your phone screen has millions of these pixels, each controlled independently.
analogy: Like pointillist paintings made of tiny colored dots. Up close you see dots, from a distance you see the picture.
example: A 1920x1080 screen has about 2 million pixels. Each updates 60+ times per second. That's 120 million color calculations per second just for display.
why_it_matters: Understanding pixels helps you understand resolution, image quality, and why some images look blocky when enlarged.
checkpoint_question: Why do images look blurry when you zoom in too much?
expected_answer: You're making each pixel bigger. The image has a fixed number of pixels. Zooming doesn't add detail - it just makes the existing dots larger and more visible.
common_mistake: Thinking higher resolution is always better. More pixels need more processing power and storage. Match resolution to your actual needs.
key_insight: RGB: Red + Green = Yellow. Red + Blue = Magenta. All three at full = White. All off = Black. That's how screens make every color.

title: The Fetch-Execute Cycle
explanation: The CPU works in a loop: fetch an instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it, repeat. Billions of times per second. Every program, every app, runs through this simple cycle.
analogy: Like a chef with a recipe: read the next step (fetch), understand it (decode), do it (execute), move to the next step. Repeat until done.
example: Instruction: 'ADD 5 to register A'. Fetch: read this from memory. Decode: understand it's addition. Execute: do the math. Store: save result. Next instruction.
why_it_matters: This cycle is why CPU speed matters. A 3GHz processor does 3 billion cycles per second. More cycles = faster programs.
checkpoint_question: Why do computers need to decode instructions?
expected_answer: Instructions are stored as binary codes. The CPU must interpret what each code means - is it add, subtract, load, store? Decoding translates the code into action.
common_mistake: Thinking faster clock speed always means faster programs. Modern CPUs do multiple things per cycle and have other bottlenecks like memory speed.
key_insight: Modern CPUs overlap these stages (pipelining). While executing one instruction, they're decoding the next and fetching the one after.

title: Parallel Computing: Many Hands Make Light Work
explanation: Instead of one processor doing everything sequentially, parallel computing uses multiple processors working simultaneously. Your phone has multiple CPU cores; graphics cards have thousands of small processors.
analogy: One person can only chop so fast. Put 10 people chopping vegetables and you finish 10x faster - if the work can be divided.
example: Video encoding: split the video into sections, process each on a different core simultaneously. What took 1 hour on one core takes minutes on eight.
why_it_matters: CPU speeds plateaued around 2005. Since then, we get more cores instead of faster cores. Understanding parallelism is essential for modern computing.
checkpoint_question: Why can't all programs run faster with more cores?
expected_answer: Some work must be done in sequence - you can't start step 2 until step 1 finishes. Tasks that depend on each other can't be parallelized. Only independent work benefits from more cores.
common_mistake: Assuming more cores always helps. Many programs are single-threaded and only use one core. Adding cores doesn't help them.
key_insight: GPUs have thousands of tiny cores for graphics. AI training uses GPUs because neural networks involve massive parallel calculations.

title: Digital vs Analog
explanation: Analog signals vary continuously (like a dimmer switch). Digital signals are discrete steps (like an on/off switch). Computers use digital because discrete values are easier to store precisely and copy perfectly.
analogy: Analog is like a ramp - infinite positions. Digital is like stairs - distinct steps. Stairs are easier to describe precisely ('step 5').
example: Vinyl records are analog - continuous grooves. CDs are digital - samples taken 44,100 times per second, each stored as a number.
why_it_matters: Understanding this explains why digital copies are perfect (copying numbers exactly) while analog degrades (noise accumulates with each copy).
checkpoint_question: Why can you copy a digital file perfectly but not an analog tape?
expected_answer: Digital files are numbers. Copy 42, you get exactly 42. Analog copies the continuous signal, but noise and imperfections sneak in. Each analog copy degrades slightly.
common_mistake: Thinking analog is worse. Analog captures continuous reality. Digital samples it. With high enough sampling rate, digital is indistinguishable to humans.
key_insight: Your microphone captures analog sound waves, converts to digital for storage, then converts back to analog for speakers. Analog-to-digital conversion happens constantly.

title: Bits and Bytes
explanation: A bit is a single 1 or 0. Eight bits make a byte. A byte can represent 256 different values (2^8). File sizes are measured in bytes: kilobyte (1000 bytes), megabyte (million), gigabyte (billion), terabyte (trillion).
analogy: Bits are like single light switches. A byte is a row of 8 switches - 256 possible patterns. More switches = more possible combinations.
example: A character takes 1 byte. A page of text ~2KB. A photo ~2MB. A movie ~2GB. A hard drive ~2TB. Each step is roughly 1000x bigger.
why_it_matters: Understanding data sizes helps you estimate storage needs and understand why some files are huge and others are tiny.
checkpoint_question: Why can a byte represent exactly 256 values?
expected_answer: 8 bits, each can be 0 or 1. That's 2×2×2×2×2×2×2×2 = 2^8 = 256 combinations. From 00000000 to 11111111.
common_mistake: Confusing bits and bytes. Internet speeds are often in megaBITS (Mb), storage in megaBYTES (MB). 8 Mb/s = 1 MB/s.
key_insight: KB/MB/GB officially use 1000, but computers often use 1024 (2^10). A 'gigabyte' drive might show as 931GB because of this difference.

title: How Computers Add Numbers
explanation: Computers add using logic gates. A 'half adder' adds two bits using AND and XOR gates. Chain them together for larger numbers. All math - multiplication, division, everything - builds from simple addition circuits.
analogy: Like doing long addition by hand, but each column is handled by a tiny circuit. Carry the 1 is a real electrical signal passing between circuits.
example: Add 5+3 in binary: 101 + 011 = 1000 (which is 8). Each bit column uses an adder circuit. Carries propagate left just like decimal addition.
why_it_matters: Understanding this demystifies computers. They're not magic - just clever arrangements of simple on/off switches doing basic logic.
checkpoint_question: Why can computers do math if they only understand on/off?
expected_answer: Numbers are represented in binary. Addition is done with logic gates (AND, OR, XOR). Complex operations are built from simple logic. On/off is enough when cleverly combined.
common_mistake: Thinking computers have special math hardware. CPUs do have optimized circuits, but fundamentally it's all logic gates.
key_insight: A modern CPU has billions of transistors. But they're all just doing AND, OR, NOT operations incredibly fast.

title: Cache: Fast Memory for Common Data
explanation: Cache is small, super-fast memory close to the CPU. It stores recently used data so the CPU doesn't wait for slow main memory. If data is in cache (hit), instant access. If not (miss), wait for RAM.
analogy: Like keeping frequently used tools on your desk instead of the garage. Walking to the garage (RAM) is slow. Reaching across your desk (cache) is instant.
example: You're editing a document. The current paragraph is in cache - typing is instant. Jump to page 100? Cache miss - brief pause while loading from RAM.
why_it_matters: Cache is why modern CPUs feel fast despite RAM being relatively slow. Understanding cache explains some performance patterns.
checkpoint_question: Why not make all memory as fast as cache?
expected_answer: Fast memory is expensive and physically large. CPU caches are megabytes, RAM is gigabytes. You can't afford or fit gigabytes of cache. The hierarchy (cache→RAM→disk) balances speed, size, and cost.
common_mistake: Assuming RAM is fast enough. For CPU-intensive work, cache behavior dominates performance. Data locality matters.
key_insight: CPUs have multiple cache levels: L1 (tiny, fastest), L2 (larger, fast), L3 (even larger, slower but still faster than RAM).

title: State: What the Computer Remembers
explanation: State is all the information a computer currently holds: variable values, which function is running, what's in memory. Programs transform state. Understanding state helps you understand how programs behave.
analogy: Like the current position of all pieces on a chess board. The state determines what moves are legal and what happens next.
example: Shopping cart contents are state. Logged-in user is state. Current page is state. Every click changes the state.
why_it_matters: Bugs often come from unexpected state. Understanding state helps you debug and design better programs.
checkpoint_question: Why is managing state difficult?
expected_answer: State can be modified from many places. It's easy to lose track of what changed it. Multiple parts of code sharing state can interfere with each other. State makes programs hard to reason about.
common_mistake: Using too much global state. When everything can change everything, bugs are hard to track. Keep state local and explicit.
code:
# State is what changes over time
counter = 0        # State: counter value

def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1   # Modifying state

# After increment(), state changed
# The program 'remembers' the new value

# Stateless function: same input = same output
def add(a, b):
    return a + b  # No state, just computation
key_insight: Functional programming minimizes state, making code easier to reason about. Each function depends only on its inputs, not hidden state.

title: Latency vs Throughput
explanation: Latency is how long one thing takes. Throughput is how many things per second. You can have high throughput with high latency (assembly line), or low latency with low throughput (custom work). Different optimizations.
analogy: Latency: how long your pizza takes to arrive. Throughput: how many pizzas the shop makes per hour. A busy shop has high throughput but your wait (latency) might be long.
example: Web server: latency is response time (200ms). Throughput is requests per second (1000 req/s). Both matter - users want fast responses AND the server must handle load.
why_it_matters: Different applications prioritize differently. Games need low latency. Batch processing needs high throughput. Know what your system needs.
checkpoint_question: A system handles 1000 requests/second but each takes 2 seconds. Is this good?
expected_answer: High throughput (1000/s is good) but high latency (2s is slow for users). Good for batch processing, bad for interactive applications. You need both metrics to evaluate.
common_mistake: Optimizing only throughput. Users feel latency. A system handling millions of requests doesn't matter if each user waits 30 seconds.
key_insight: Little's Law: average items in system = throughput × latency. If latency doubles, you need twice the capacity to maintain throughput.
